title: Make Money Online: Web Skills, Real Wages, and a Work Plan
description:
Making money online starts with work someone needs, not a guaranteed-income promise. Using supplied BLS figures for May 2025, this video compares U.S. median employee wages for web developers ($92,650 a year) and web and digital-interface designers ($104,000 a year), then shows their May 2024 comparisons. We explain why those wages are not freelance earnings or a promise of remote work, unpack projected openings and growth, and build a practical plan: choose a skill, create a focused sample, define a small service, approach potential clients, and set clear payment terms. Which skill would you start with, and what would your first project be?

For entertainment and informational purposes only. This is not financial, legal, medical, or other professional advice. Consult a qualified professional about your circumstances. We are not responsible for decisions or results based on this video.

scenes.text: For your planning, the important boundary is self-employment. These employee wage figures exclude it, so don't label them typical freelance income or business profit.
scenes.subject: independent contractor

scenes.text: A freelance project's payment has to cover more than building the page. Think about client messages, revisions, software expenses, and time spent finding work.
scenes.subject: freelancer planning

scenes.text: Use wage data to understand an occupation's scale, not to set a guaranteed target. Your actual offer or project agreement determines what you receive.

scenes.text: U.S. web-developer and digital-designer occupations are projected to average 13,600 job openings per year from 2025 through 2035. That's an outlook, not today's vacancy count.
scenes.subject: recruitment meeting

visual.headline: RECRUITMENT MEETING
visual.sub: That's an outlook, not today's vacancy count.

scenes.text: Employment in the combined occupations is projected to grow 5% across 2025 through 2035. That percentage covers the full period, not each individual year.
scenes.subject: development team

visual.headline: PROJECTED EMPLOYMENT GROWTH
visual.sub: U.S. combined occupations • 2025–2035, full period • BLS

scenes.text: Neither projection tells you how many openings are remote, beginner-friendly, or freelance. Treat demand as context, then investigate the requirements of actual opportunities.
scenes.subject: job searcher

scenes.text: Now choose the work you want to practice. Development means making a website function; design emphasizes the layout and interactions people use to navigate.
scenes.subject: website workshop

visual.headline: CHOOSE THE WORK TO PRACTICE
visual.sub: Now choose the work you want to practice.

scenes.text: Try a small practice task before buying an expensive course. Build a simple page, or redesign a confusing screen, and notice which work holds your attention.
scenes.subject: coding learner

visual.headline: TRY A SMALL PRACTICE TASK
visual.sub: Try a small practice task before buying an expensive course.

scenes.text: You don't need to promise a complete business transformation. Start by identifying a concrete website problem you can explain, practice solving, and eventually demonstrate.
scenes.subject: website evaluation

scenes.text: Here's a practical sample idea: a simple service-business website that clearly explains the offer, displays contact information, and works comfortably on a phone.
scenes.subject: website prototype

scenes.text: Make it an honestly labeled practice project. Don't invent a paying client, customer testimonial, or sales improvement to make your portfolio look more established.
scenes.subject: portfolio editor

visual.headline: LABEL PRACTICE WORK HONESTLY
visual.sub: Make it an honestly labeled practice project.

scenes.text: For development, demonstrate the actual behavior: navigation that works, readable content on smaller screens, and form checks that help people correct mistakes before submitting.
scenes.subject: website testing

scenes.text: For design, explain your choices. Show how the page directs attention, where the main action belongs, and why the text is easier to read.
scenes.subject: layout presentation

visual.headline: EXPLAIN YOUR DESIGN CHOICES
visual.sub: For design, explain your choices.

scenes.text: Ask someone to try a specific task, like finding the contact information. Watch where they hesitate. Their feedback gives you something concrete to improve.
scenes.subject: usability tester

visual.headline: WATCH A REAL TASK
visual.sub: Watch where they hesitate.

scenes.text: Then document the problem, your changes, and what you tested. A clear explanation makes your sample easier to evaluate than a screenshot without context.
scenes.subject: portfolio writer

scenes.text: Before we continue, what's your opinion? What website task frustrates you most on your phone?

scenes.text: An offer should describe something deliverable, not just say you do websites. For example, propose a mobile-friendly service page using the client's approved text.
scenes.subject: proposal writer

visual.headline: SELL A DEFINED DELIVERABLE
visual.sub: Suggested offer, not a guaranteed sale

scenes.text: Write down what is included and excluded. A page redesign doesn't automatically include photography, ongoing updates, hosting, or writing every word for the business.
scenes.subject: scope discussion

visual.headline: DEFINE WHAT IS INCLUDED
visual.sub: Agree on inclusion or exclusion

scenes.text: Price the actual scope rather than copying an annual employee wage. Estimate your work, include project expenses, and decide whether the terms are worthwhile.
scenes.subject: project estimator

scenes.text: Before starting, agree on deliverables, deadlines, revision limits, and payment terms in writing. Clear expectations help both sides understand what finishing the project means.
scenes.subject: agreement meeting

scenes.text: For employee roles, take a different route: match your portfolio to the job description. Show relevant work, and be direct about your current experience.
scenes.subject: application reviewer

scenes.text: Don't claim tools you can't use or results you didn't achieve. A modest, explainable sample is something you can discuss honestly in an interview.
scenes.subject: portfolio interview

scenes.text: Before we continue, what's your opinion? Which project term would you clarify first: scope or payment?

scenes.text: Start outreach with relevance. If a business publicly invites inquiries, introduce yourself briefly, explain a specific website issue, and ask whether they'd consider help.
scenes.subject: outreach writer

visual.headline: MAKE YOUR OUTREACH RELEVANT
visual.sub: Start outreach with relevance.

scenes.text: Keep the claim narrow. You can offer to improve a confusing layout without promising more customers, higher revenue, or a particular position in search results.
scenes.subject: website consultant

visual.headline: PROMISE WORK, NOT GUARANTEED REVENUE
visual.sub: Keep the claim narrow.

scenes.text: Share a relevant sample rather than a pile of unrelated links. Let the person see the kind of problem you can handle and your reasoning.
scenes.subject: portfolio walkthrough

scenes.text: If someone is interested, ask about their goals, existing website access, and who approves changes. Don't request passwords casually or alter anything without permission.
scenes.subject: project discovery

scenes.text: Keep records of your proposals, agreements, expenses, and payments. That helps you understand the business side instead of confusing an incoming payment with take-home income.
scenes.subject: freelance bookkeeping

scenes.text: If outreach doesn't lead to work, review the fit, sample, and offer. Rejection alone doesn't tell you which part needs improvement, so avoid expensive guesswork.
scenes.subject: proposal revision

scenes.text: Your starting plan is straightforward: choose development or design, practice a narrow task, and produce a sample you can explain. Use that sample to support applications or a clearly scoped service offer.
scenes.subject: skills planner

scenes.text: Keep your spending connected to a real need. Before purchasing software or training, identify the task it will help you complete and whether an available alternative would let you practice first.
scenes.subject: training comparison

visual.headline: SPEND FOR A DEFINED NEED
visual.sub: Keep your spending connected to a real need.

scenes.text: The practical takeaway is simple: turn a web skill into evidence of useful work, then seek a real agreement. The wage figures describe occupations; they don't promise your personal earnings.
